slides.text: Working the night shift at the old city archive is usually a masterclass in boredom. Just me, a thermos of black coffee, and a wall of silent CCTV monitors showing dusty, empty hallways. At 3:14 AM, I saw her on camera four. A woman in a torn red dress, standing motionless at the end of the basement corridor. My heart hammered against my ribs. The building was on absolute lockdown. Nobody could have gotten inside.

I grabbed my heavy flashlight and radio, rushing down three flights of stairs to the basement. I swept the pitch-black corridor with my beam. Empty. The thick dust on the concrete floor was completely undisturbed. I radioed the front desk to check if anyone else was in the building. Only static answered. Shaking my head at my own paranoia, I trudged back up to the security room to check the playback on the camera system.

I rewound the footage from camera four. The woman in red was there. But she wasn't standing in the basement hallway. As I watched the screen closer, I noticed the reflection of the glowing exit sign behind her. It was backwards. The camera wasn't facing the basement. The camera was mounted directly above my desk. I slowly turned my chair around. The woman in the torn red dress was standing right behind me.
